column3: Shares the victory root, but describes luxuriant gardens rather than military defeat or reversal.
Its increased bodily strength gives only a broad contrast to the Romans' defeated condition.
It states that God's forces are the victors, directly opposing the focus's condition of defeat.
Uses the same defeat verb for people overcome by their misery, preserving defeat as a condition rather than an identity.
Immediate continuation: the defeated Romans are explicitly promised a later victory.
Foretells that deniers will be defeated, supplying a clear but differently framed reversal of power.
God's help makes a people victorious, directly supplying the victorious counterpart to the focus.
Immediate continuation grounds the predicted reversal in God's unfailing promise.
Makes victory and defeat contingent on divine help or its withdrawal, explaining the focus's changing power.
A small group overcomes a larger one by God's permission, showing victory need not follow apparent strength.
Its disclosure of disputed truth and exposure of lying has no specific defeat or reversal connection.
God's written decree that He and His messengers will prevail directly supports the promised reversal.
The descent of the trustworthy Spirit does not clarify the Romans' defeat or future victory.
Creation and return establish divine power broadly, but do not develop the military reversal.
It identifies God's party as victorious, a relevant divine-allegiance account of prevailing.
The divine name alone does not clarify defeat, victory, or their reversal.

The request for delay does not clarify defeat or future victory.
